body.title: Rajput Stone Citadel Hydraulics: Maota Lake and the Water Lifts of Amer
body.orientation: How engineering genius lifted water hundreds of feet up rocky cliffs to nourish gardens and palaces in the arid desert hills.

hero.alt: Amer Fort ramparts reflected in the waters of Maota Lake

paragraphs.text: Amer Fort, constructed primarily of red sandstone and marble by Raja Man Singh I beginning in 1592, served as the royal seat of the Kachwaha dynasty before the founding of Jaipur.
The greatest architectural feat of the citadel was its multi-stage Persian wheel hydraulic system that lifted water from Maota Lake up nearly 400 feet into the fort's storage tanks.
The lifted water powered fountains in the Sheesh Mahal and cascaded through marble channels into the Kesar Kyari saffron garden laid out in the middle of Maota Lake.
Amer's water architecture demonstrates that medieval Indian hill citadels were sophisticated ecological habitats harmonizing defence, water harvesting, and microclimate regulation.

claims.text: Amer Fort was constructed by Raja Man Singh I as the fortified capital of the Kachwaha Rajputs.

evidence.excerpt: Amer Fort was built by Raja Man Singh I in the late 16th century, situated high on a hill overlooking Maota Lake.

claims.text: Water was lifted from the lake to the summit fort through multi-tiered pulley and aqueduct systems.

evidence.excerpt: A complex system of Persian wheels (rehats) lifted water from Maota Lake across multiple terrace levels into the upper citadel reservoirs.

claims.text: The lake water irrigated the geometrically designed Kesar Kyari island garden.

evidence.excerpt: In the center of Maota Lake lies the Kesar Kyari garden, created with star-shaped sunken flower beds.

claims.text: The water system moderated desert summer temperatures inside the residential pavilions.

evidence.excerpt: Circulating water through hidden wall channels and cooling screens allowed inhabitants to withstand intense summer heat.
